#6673. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6669. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6668. Exclusive: Shohei Ohtani Just Signed a Historic Deal With New Balance

Shohei Ohtani is used to making history. In addition to his four MLB MVP awards and two World Series rings, the Los Angeles Dodgers two-way great is the first member of the 50/50 club (having racked up 54 home runs and 59 stolen bases during the 2024 season), became the first player to hit three homers and record 10 strikeouts in a single game (which he managed in a 2025 NLCS contest against the Brewers), and earlier this year maintained simultaneous streaks in games on base (48) and innings without an earned run (32 and two-thirds).

Now, the 32-year-old Japanese icon is adding to those accolades with a pioneering endorsement deal, officially extending his relationship with his longtime partner New Balance through to the end of his baseball career. (While a rarefied group of athletes have signed lifetime sponsorship deals—including LeBron James and Cristiano Ronaldo at Nike, and Damian Lillard at Adidas—Ohtani’s new contract appears to be both the first to exclusively cover a star’s playing days and the first of its kind in MLB.)

“There’s a lot of trust,” Ohtani tells me through an interpreter during a sit-down in Boston of his decision to commit to the New England sportswear stalwart for the long haul. “We’ve obviously built friendships, as well. They’ve been able to accommodate my requests, the things I’ve asked for, and, like I said, that takes the involvement of a lot of trust. That relationship has been very, very good and smooth. I had no reservations about extending our relationship.”

Earlier in the day, I shadowed Ohtani at New Balance’s headquarters, where, as part of the agreement, the company is renaming its on-site think tank as the Shohei Ohtani Sports Research Lab. A team of specialists led the Dodgers superstar through a slew of shoes—including his on-field Ohtani 1 model, which will receive new editions in 2027—and then a rack of branded apparel. All of it falls under his Shohei Ohtani Signature Collection, which New Balance launched in 2024 (about a year and a half after the athlete first signed with the company). The collection has grown deliberately and unhurriedly ever since—mirroring his patience in the batter’s box; Ohtani is methodical when it comes to product development and uninterested in rolling out rushed goods with his name slapped on them.

While conducting a kind of footwear postmortem on his 2026 season—which started well, but ended with a rare slump (and left knee and right biceps injuries that kept him from pitching after July 3)—Ohtani noted there’d been some moments of slippage on the heel of his landing foot when pitching. On a printed-out diagram, he used a pencil to sketch ways in which the shoe’s spikes might be slightly reconfigured to find a sweet spot for stability on the mound and speed around the bases. The question of switching footwear between pitching and batting comes up, but Ohtani has not yet done this (and it seems the consensus is to stick with one shoe only).

“I have a lot of direct input into the footwear and apparel,” Ohtani says. “That includes my style, which I like to keep simple, as well as performance-based requests, [like with my] spikes. Some years we make minor changes, and sometimes we’ll make a big change. They understand what I want.”

Ohtani’s apparel line runs across three categories: performance, lifestyle, and fanwear. His custom logo—a striking ink drawing of his figure, designed by the Japanese manga artist Takehiko Inoue—is featured subtly on the bulk of the lineup. “Shohei doesn’t see himself as a glamorous player,” Chris Davis, New Balance brand president and chief marketing officer, tells me. “He sees himself as a gritty, hardworking athlete who wants to get better every day, and his logo reflects this—it has this kind of quiet intensity.”

While some of the future apparel designs boast cool technical features—like detachable, two-in-one, and reversible elements inspired by Ohtani’s two-way play—the man himself is only concerned that his products “fit comfortably and to be easy to wear.” When asked if there’s anyone whose style he likes or is influenced by, Ohtani shrugs. “Honestly, not really. I just like to wear what I like to wear.”

“[Shohei] is very quick and clear with his input,” says Masahiro Uchida, New Balance’s general manager of athlete signature product, who has worked alongside Ohtani for years. “On the performance side, he always prefers softness and a soft hand feel. For the lifestyle side, he prefers clean and simple. He also understands the occasion. He always asks us, ‘Where would I wear this?’” One major goal for Ohtani with his apparel, Uchida adds, is to “support the expansion of baseball culture and show his respect for its heritage. He is a super geek about MLB. He knows so much.”

At 32, the duration of Ohtani’s career—and, now, his New Balance deal—remains an open question. That age can be considered as getting toward the older end in pro baseball, but elite pitchers have a habit of playing well into their 40s—Justin Verlander, for example, just pitched his final season at 43.

Ohtani still plans on being a full two-way player in 2027, with hopes for a Cy Young Award—MLB’s top pitching honor, one of the few laurels he has yet to win—still alive. When the Dodgers’ season ended on October 15, Ohtani told the press that he was “not quite satisfied with how things shaped up on the pitching side.”

What words of advice or motivation does he have, I ask, for the legion of kids hoping to follow in his footsteps? His answer feels like something he might be saying to himself as the next season approaches.

“If you want to become successful, baseball is a sport that takes a lot of repetitive practice,” he says. “You always have to work on your fundamentals. Once you reach a certain level, the sport becomes very, very hard. At that point, you need to remember why you’re playing. Are you playing because you love the sport? If you have that drive, that love for it, then even when it’s tough, you can overcome it.”

#6667. Taylor Swift Is at Travis Kelce’s Chiefs-Cardinals Game—and Made It a Family Affair

Taylor Swift has been spotted at all of Travis Kelce’s home games this season, and today’s matchup against the Arizona Cardinals was no exception. The singer was photographed with her parents, Andrea and Scott Swift, as she cheered on the Kansas City Chiefs. She wore a red and black jacket.

Swift has been out of the public eye since Wednesday, when she performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years. She attended the ceremony with Kelce’s teammate Patrick Mahomes’s wife, Brittany Mahomes.

Neither Kelce nor Patrick was with them at the ceremony, as the two NFL players are in the middle of their season.

Kelce has also been recovering from an ankle injury that sidelined him for part of the Chiefs’ game against the Atlanta Falcons last Sunday.

After the game, he told USA Today that he was doing fine. “I’m all good,” he said. “I probably could have done more than I did when I came back, but it was the direction the team wanted to go, so I was right there with them. We had a lot of young guys step up, so it was really nice.”

In March, the 37-year-old tight end spoke on The Pat McAfee Show about how Swift inspired him to play another season.

He said that “without a doubt [watching her be on top of her field motivated me to continue playing]. We share the same love for what we do and fortunately, we’ve had this desire since we were kids in our selective professions.”

“It’s just amazing to see her keep going to the table,” he said of her music career. “Keep finding new things to write about. Keep finding new melodies and things like that. And on top of that, still seeing her have that love and joy in what she does, of course that’s motivating. That’s motivating for anyone to see, let alone you know, [me watching] my fiancée and knowing that I’m going through something where I’m trying to figure out exactly what the future holds for me. Something like that definitely motivates me to say, ‘You know what? I’m not done either. I’ve still got some ideas in the back of my mind. I’ve still got some juice left to play this game.’”

#6666. These Cozy Casseroles Are Perfect For Feeding A Crowd This Holiday (And Beyond!)

Casseroles remind me of cuddling up at home by the fire with my loved ones and digging into the tastiest dishes. They're also some of the easiest recipes to throw together in no time, and are the best for serving a holiday crowd. What else could you want? Now that we're firmly in the cold season, I can't stop craving them, so obviously, I turn to my favorite Delish recipes to make it happen. This holiday season, make sure to try out these 12 casserole recipes for some of the best bites you'll have all season. We have some classics, like a comforting chicken and rice casserole that'll have you dreaming of home, alongside more inventive and mouthwatering dishes like our French onion croissant strata.

There are few pairings as classic as meatloaf and mashed potatoes, but this casserole is anything but basic. Take your side of mashed potatoes, stack it on top of your meatloaf, and load it up with all of your favorite baked potato toppings. You’ll have an indulgent, craveable casserole that turns into the best leftovers—if you have any.

When you’re hungry for something that’s comforting, cozy, and a little luxe feeling too, chicken Marsala is a truly excellent option. The pan sauce has plenty of mushrooms, fortified Marsala wine, and a splash of cream, because why not? It’s a fantastic dinner, easy enough for a weeknight and special enough for date night.

A breakfast strata is one of our go-tos when we want a hearty, shareable brunch dish, but it’s hard to put into words how good this French onion croissant strata is. It takes a few extra minutes to deeply caramelize the onions, but the extra flavor and richness make a HUGE difference.

Chicken soup is a comfort food icon, good for the soul and the stomach, and there are a world’s worth of chicken soup recipes to choose from. Take chicken, egg noodles, some veggies, and a creamy sauce and bake them into a hearty casserole? You have a hearty dinner that leads to full bellies and happy hearts.

This slow-cooker casserole, featuring potatoes, beans, corn, and lots of cheese, is hearty, packed with flavor, and sure to make repeat appearances on your grub rotation all fall long.

Chicken and broccoli casserole is a meal that most people at Team Delish grew up eating, and this recipe is guaranteed to make you feel like a kid again. This creamy, cheesy, Ritz cracker-topped casserole is packed with chicken, rice, and freshly blanched broccoli with the quintessential cream of mushroom soup.

When it comes to this casserole, think breakfast strata with buttery, caramelized apples, and lots of sharp cheddar. If you’re in need of a quick fall-forward recipe to throw together for a weekend brunch, you can easily turn to this one.

When we need a direct flight to a quick and easy dinner destination, we turn to two trusty options: a casserole or a chicken dinner. This chicken and rice casserole is the best of both worlds. It requires minimal cleanup, and the hands-on cooking time is only 20 minutes. The rest of the time, you can just lounge in your living room while this whips itself up.

When the weather gets cold, your dinner making-mojo is low, or when comfort food is just what’s on the menu, you need a casserole. Even though we have loved so many other casseroles before, there's always room in my baking dish for one more. And if that casserole is easy, creamy, chicken-y, and cheesy? With a crunchy topping? Our oven is already preheating.

Watch out, classic green bean casserole, gnocchi has entered the holiday menu. We took the classic recipe and added gnocchi for a dish that's infinitely better than the sum of its parts. Blanched fresh green beans and buttery sliced mushrooms, onions, and garlic get tossed with a creamy béchamel sauce and pillowy gnocchi, then baked until bubbly.

This enchilada casserole is what weeknight dinner dreams are made of. Classic chicken enchiladas are a fan-favorite meal, but they can be kind of tedious to prepare when you're low on energy (all that rolling, right?). In this recipe, you just layer all your components in a casserole dish, bake until melty and saucy, add your desired toppings, and serve!

In our book, it doesn't get more comforting than shepherd's pie. Because this meat and potatoes dish is such a classic, we spent a while perfecting the comfort food staple—your weeknights should be as cozy as possible.

#6665. New Orleans Guide: Where to Stay, Eat, Drink, and Revel in the Big Easy

A bastion of hedonism, New Orleans is where indulgence is expected, revelry encouraged, and a good time all but guaranteed. Without question, eating and drinking is part and parcel of any visit to the Big Easy—but the city’s culture extends far beyond beignets and Sazeracs, converting first-time visitors into lifelong devotees of its countless charms. All it takes is a stroll down its oak-lined avenues to spark a love affair with New Orleans. It happened to me—and over a decade later I’m still hypnotized, returning to the Crescent City year after year to get my fix.

For centuries, New Orleans has played host to literary giants and jazz luminaries, civil rights leaders, and iconic artists. It’s a mysterious place where funerals become parades, Voodoo is still practiced, and tombs are above ground. Adding to its uniqueness, the city winds along the Mississippi River and is surrounded by wetland habitats of swamps, bayous, and marshes.

The oldest neighborhood here is the French Quarter (also known as Vieux Carré), which despite its reputation for rowdy tourists and souvenir shops, is tightly woven into the tapestry of New Orleans culture (read: don’t skip it). But you shouldn’t stop there—the Marigny, Bywater, Tremé, Garden District, Bayou St. John, Freret, and Algiers Point (among others) should also be on your radar when curating an itinerary.

Whether you’re planning a first-time visit or returning for an annual pilgrimage, laissez les bon temps rouler with the ultimate New Orleans travel guide below.

Experiencing New Orleans by foot is quintessential. Thanks to flat terrain, compact neighborhoods, and several pedestrian-friendly streets, it ranks high in walkability. If you plan to use the streetcar to get around (another great option relied upon by tourists and locals alike), download the Le Pass app to search for schedules and purchase your ticket ahead of time. (If you don’t, be sure to bring exact change—$1.25—with you.) There are five different streetcar lines, the historic, open-air Saint Charles Line being the most charming (more on that ahead). Rideshares like Lyft and Uber are also available in New Orleans.

The best time to visit New Orleans depends on your travel goals. If pleasant weather is your prerogative, spring and fall will both be cool and comfortable. For those eager to join Mardi Gras festivities, late winter will be your best bet, whereas if you prefer the spooky vibes, October can’t be beat. For die-hard cocktail lovers willing to brave the heat, come in July when Tales of the Cocktail takes place. And if you’re keen to see the city festooned in lights and garlands, come for the holiday season.

You can almost imagine what it felt like to stroll through its glamorous halls when The Pontchartrain Hotel originally opened its doors in 1927. This Garden District icon (which began as a luxury apartment building but converted to a hotel in the ‘40s) clutches onto its nostalgic charm with details like the lobby’s original terrazzo floor, heavy velvet drapes, and gleaming crystal chandeliers. (Not to mention the hotel key cabinet behind the front desk.) The original owners allowed long-term guests to haul in their own furniture and decor, and that pied-à-terre flair lingers throughout the suites and guest rooms. There are four food and beverage spaces in the hotel: the Hot-Tin Rooftop Bar, their fine dining concept Jack Rose, The Silver Whistle Café, and the Bayou Bar for Creole-inspired dishes and live jazz. Previous guests include Truman Capote, Frank Sinatra, The Doors, and Tennessee Williams, who worked on A Streetcar Named Desire during his residency here.

Located in the Marigny (the French Quarter’s quieter, calmer neighbor), this boutique property from Ash Hotels is set within a former Catholic church that was erected in the 19th century. The rooms (each individually decorated) stretch across three different historic buildings: the schoolhouse, the rectory, and the convent. (There’s also the brick church next door with its stained glass windows and restored murals that is now used as an event space.) This is no doubt an aesthete’s hotel—there are over 700 antiques throughout the expertly curated spaces, as well as furnishings produced locally. (Don’t miss the cypress double staircase by the front desk; it will take your breath away.) From limestone clawfoot tubs, sumptuous canopy beds, and perfectly mismatched upholstery, a stay at Hotel Peter and Paul is right in step with what makes New Orleans a destination with distinction.

For those naysayers who profess they’ll never stay overnight in the boisterous French Quarter, The Celestine has other plans for you. This 14-room boutique hotel strikes a fetching balance between modern creature comforts and old-world charm (think: antiques and four-poster beds puzzled together with Dr. Vranjes toiletries and a curated wet bar)—and the interior courtyard set to the gurgling tunes of its three-tier fountain offers a slowed-down pace to immerse in the old city. The building dates back to 1791 and was once the home of Antoine Amédée Peychaud (founder of Peychaud’s bitters, father of the Sazerac cocktail) and his wife, Celestine. Tennessee Williams also stayed here when he was working on A Streetcar Named Desire in the 1940s, and his former suite has been converted into the hotel’s lobby. While here, don’t miss out on Peychaud’s Bar, where guests and passersby alike can enjoy a reserve cocktail dreamt up by Neal Bodenheimer from Cure Co.

If it wasn’t already obvious, the hotel scene in New Orleans is one of the very best in the country. But if you find yourself strolling along the city’s sidewalks, admiring the Queen Anne architecture of the Garden District, or the Creole cottages throughout The Bywater, a stay with Dear Valentine offers the best of both worlds. Founder Melissa Shelton snapped up a collection of homes throughout the city—each with architectural and historical significance—collaborating with conservationists, interior designers, and local artisans to create a compelling brand. On a recent visit, I stayed at Dear Valentine’s Bouligny Victorian property uptown. The imaginative design by Logan Killen Interiors made each day feel like opening the door to a jewel box (a very large, two-story jewel box), and the private backyard with a plunge pool offered respite after hours of walking. Thoughtful touches—keyless locks, a washer and dryer, and a massive chef’s kitchen—felt like home. But with the option to add on a private chef, grocery delivery, or a concierge, hotel-caliber services are also at your fingertips. Dear Valentine homes range in size and can accommodate between 4 and 42 people, making it an obvious pick for group travel.

As with so many historic hotels in New Orleans, Columns has toggled through several previous lives—first as a private residence, then as a boarding house during World War I, and finally as a hotel (which is now listed on the National Register of Historic Places). Locals know and love Columns for its massive porch—which becomes particularly lively during weekend brunch—and the interiors retain that private residence feel for guests, from toile wallpaper and stone fireplaces to a mahogany staircase that climbs upwards to reveal a stained-glass skylight. When you’re hungry (and thirsty), head for the bar (or garden) for a cocktail, followed by dinner at the restaurant helmed by executive chef Paul Terrebonne.

This 14-room boutique hotel tucked in the heart of the leafy Garden District is brought to you by local hospitality veterans, LeBlanc + Smith. The first thing you’ll notice upon arrival is the structure—it’s housed within a 19th-century mansion that’s been painted a shadowy slate blue. Similarly, the walls in the interior public spaces are tinted in deep jewel tones and decorated with a textural mix of clever antiques (e.g., a wood-carved birdcage) and vintage objects. There’s an all-day restaurant with both indoor and outdoor seating (the focaccia with goat cheese and olive oil is a must), a stylish lobby bar where you can pull up a stool or take your cocktail out onto the front porch, and out back, you’ll find a pool with an adjacent bar serving up small bites and tropical drinks.

A grand dame of New Orleans, this magnificent property opened its doors in 1893 as the Grunewald Hotel, eventually coming to bear its current moniker in honor of former president Theodore Roosevelt in 1923. Stepping into the gilded, block-long lobby with its soaring ceilings and 1867-era Eugène Farcot clock, guests are ushered back in time. Dive deeper into the hotel’s history with a visit to The Sazerac Bar, an iconic watering hole from the 1940s with well-preserved Art Deco design. Also not to be missed: the extensive salumi menu at the property’s Domenica restaurant, plus a bit of pampering at the Waldorf Astoria Spa (complete with a glass of welcome Champagne).

Well positioned within the Warehouse District, this elegant hotel (formerly Maison de la Luz) was built in the early 1900s and served as an annex to New Orleans's former city hall. Now, it’s one of the most admired boutique guesthouses in the city, offering 67 rooms. A nightly wine and cheese hour offers the opportunity to enjoy the ground-level lounge, which resembles the parlor of a well-traveled collector. (There’s also an honor bar for whipping up your own Sazerac or French 75). Stroll through to the next room, and you’ll discover the Instagram-ready breakfast nook with its blue-and-white wallpaper and towering windows. When you’re ready for a drink, slip into Salon Salon for a craft cocktail and small bites (I recommend the pommes pavé), or opt for an even more intimate setting in the guest-only speakeasy-themed bar, accessible via a bookcase door.

Despite being a city largely defined by its waterways, there aren’t a lot of hotels in the Crescent City that showcase views of the Mississippi River. Thankfully, Four Seasons Hotel New Orleans does—and quite magnificently so. The property sits along the riverbanks and soars four hundred feet into the sky, crescendoing at a 34th-floor observation deck. Among its many highlights are the rooftop swimming pool, as well as the circular Chandelier Bar in the lobby that sits beneath a glittering installation of more than 15,000 crystals (if you’re here on a Thursday, there’s live jazz from 6 to 9 p.m.). Enjoy a dinner at the property’s Miss River restaurant helmed by Chef Alon Shaya—the sweet potato brioche bread service is a must, as is the carved buttermilk-fried chicken for the table. As for accommodations, nothing beats watching Steamboat Natchez gliding by from the hotel’s gorgeous river-view suites.

New Orleans is a city abundant in historic mansions. And if you’re determined to sleep in one, I suggest you make it The Whit. This new opening on Prytania Street offers 15 rooms and suites and was named for Walt Whitman. (The poet’s three-month stay in the spring of 1848 significantly shaped “Leaves of Grass.”) The exterior of the Greek Revival mansion is imposing and impressive, guarded by palms, live oaks, and a magnificent Magnolia tree. The hotel was developed by Gretchen Trauth of ERG Enterprises, who tapped Logan Killen Interiors for the design, and a team of specialists to preserve and restore original details—like the crown molding, which, for me, resembles frosting layers on an extravagant cake. Neal Bodenheimer developed the drinks program and features tableside punches, while Brechtel Hospitality oversees the culinary experience. (I cannot stress enough how crucial it is you order the seasonal scone for breakfast.) And for couples looking for somewhere romantic to tie the knot, The Whit has positioned itself as a wedding venue with dedicated bridal suites and construction on an iron-and-glass pavilion currently underway.

Among the oldest hotels in New Orleans, this 1885 Beaux-Arts landmark is one of the city’s crown jewels. Slipping past the doors (attended to by friendly bellhops) is like stepping back in time, where coffered ceilings, sparkly chandeliers, marble floors, and a wood-carved grandfather clock greet guests. Several important authors throughout history have written about the property, thus its designation as a literary landmark, and its suites are dedicated to legends such as Truman Capote and Ernest Hemingway. Hotel Monteleone’s pièce de résistance is the Carousel Bar on the ground level, which has been rotating and serving up drinks since 1949. Securing a seat at the 24-person bar is a feat, but guests can join an early access experience with the hotel’s renowned mixologist, Marvin Allen, who regales imbibers with tales of the bar’s storied past.

It’s the facade that first grabs your attention at Hotel Saint Vincent—two levels of ornate ironwork, with a red brick edifice rising handsomely from behind. The Lower Garden District landmark first opened in 1861 as an infant asylum, funded by an Irish philanthropist named Margaret Haughery. Much later, after a complete renovation, the hotel was unveiled in 2021. The interiors by Lambert McGuire Design strike a balance between nostalgia and modernity: teak chairs sit in dialogue with vintage Murano glass chandeliers, which cast light on custom Voutsa wallpaper in a psychedelic pattern. This interplay between texture, color, and shape weaves throughout all of the hotel’s spaces, including San Lorenzo and Paradise Lounge (the seasonal Italian restaurant and lobby bar) and a moody bar named Chapel Club. Order a spritz by the pool beneath the green scalloped umbrellas, or pop into the ByGeorge boutique for an embroidered Bode shirt or locally crafted candle before retiring to one of the 75 guest rooms and suites.

The Warbler made its anticipated debut in October 2026 along St. Charles Avenue, and with it arrived Mildred’s, a martini bar and restaurant worthy of any New Orleans travel itinerary. Much like the rest of the hotel, the interiors evoke the relaxed mood of a European café, but with a colorful New Orleans twist. The menu leans in the direction of Spain and was developed in partnership with CureCo and Andrew Zimmerman of Chicago's Michelin-starred Sepia. Kick off the evening with the vermouth service, followed by a specialty martini (there are eight to choose from) paired with clam toast encrusted with garlic and Calabrian chiles.

Blink and you might miss the entrance to Patula, but that would be a shame. This new all-day cafe and wine bar is cozied away in Krewe’s courtyard, and has rapidly become a favorite among locals and visitors alike. Chef Rob Tabone is among the cast of characters revitalizing the French Quarter’s dining scene, working hand-in-hand with local farmers and purveyors to curate a menu worth singing praises about. The wine list is equally distinct, with bottles coming from small producers focused on low-intervention winemaking.

You can’t discuss the modern craft cocktail movement in New Orleans without paying tribute to Cure. Neal Bodenheimer’s beloved spot on Freret Street—opened in 2009—is now one of the most celebrated bars in the country, with accolades including a James Beard Award and multiple inclusions on 50 Best. Despite all the clout, the atmosphere at Cure is relaxed and convivial, anchored by an imposing bar and ceiling-to-floor windows. A warning: Choosing your libation will prove challenging. The rotating cocktail list is packed with mind-bending flavors and combinations that are created in collaboration with Cure’s talented team of bartenders.

Tucked inside a former pharmacy from the early 1900s, this fine dining restaurant first opened in 1982 and was named after a Louisiana-born socialite who was the muse for painter John Singer Sargent's controversial Portrait of Madame X. Executive Chef Rob Mistry’s menu reflects his global upbringing—born in New York City, raised between suburban Paris and North Carolina, and a child of Parsi parents from Mumbai. You can expect regional New Orleans ingredients, but through Mistry’s sharp point of view. The blue crab toast with sambar and cucumber—served on Japanese milk bread—is worth booking a visit to New Orleans for alone.

Allow me to introduce you to your new favorite spot to slurp down briny oysters: Holywater has arrived in the French Quarter. If the name sounds familiar, that’s because there’s already a successful Holywater outpost in New York City. But its Louisiana counterpart is distinctly its own. The three-story restaurant is family-run and sits within an 1800s maritime chandlery, attired in nautical decor aplenty. Begin the evening with an order of the caviar tater tots and super-chilled wedge salad, followed by a tower of their oysters, shrimp cocktail, and crab dip.

Opened in June 2025, this contemporary Asian restaurant by Chef Ashwin Vilkhu is a love letter to family dinners from his childhood growing up in New Orleans. The Farouki Farouki interiors are inspired by golden hour in his family’s home where he learned to cook, and the restaurant is named after the street his family lived on after they moved from New Delhi to New Orleans in the 1980s. The four-course dinner takes guests on a sensory tour of his most cherished flavors, including the crab, brie, and Champagne soup, which pairs beautifully with a crémant.

For an easygoing snack and drink, head for Bar Pomona in the Marigny. The interiors read like a countryside diner (in the best way), and on Mondays they serve up lasagna alongside natural wines from regions such as the Jura and Savoie.

If you’re not already a tiki cocktail convert, this is the place to try it. The founder, Jeff Berry, is credited with reviving vintage tiki cocktails to their original glory in the 1990s, and the menu weaves together premium spirits with compelling flavors like anise, pandan leaf extract, and almond.

This breakfast, lunch, and weekend brunch spot is close to plenty of city highlights—like Audubon Park and Magazine Street shopping—but it’s a destination in its own right. The breezy interiors and natural light make perching in a corner by the window (dressed in gingham drapes) feel especially cozy. And with dishes like the grits carbonara and huevos rotos, it’s all too easy to find yourself at Cafe Malou multiple times in one New Orleans trip.

Rightfully earning its position on The New York Times’s 2024 Best New Restaurants list, this seafood-driven Mexican spot in the Bywater neighborhood is in a league of its own. Co-owned by sisters and Mexico City natives Ana and Lydia Castro (the former a James Beard Award-nominated chef), Acamaya is one of the most exciting new additions to New Orleans’s storied hospitality scene. There’s no point giving ordering advice here—everything on the menu is just that good.

Complement a morning in City Park with a leisurely lunch at Ralph’s on the Park. Guests can tuck into white cornmeal fried oysters and a plate of shrimp & grits while gazing out at historic live oaks. If you’re lucky, you’ll meet Arthur, the restaurant’s charming-as-ever maître d’.

Caribbean flavors meet Cuban heritage at this French Quarter mainstay that’s helmed by executive chef Alfredo Nogueira. The bar has been open for over a decade, but each visit offers something new thanks to its seasonal approach to ingredients. The cocktail menu is sensational (first-timers should get the classic Hurricane & Table), and flavorful dishes like the sweet plantains and fish rundown complement each other from start to finish.

A New Orleans fine dining classic, Brennan’s has been an institution since opening in 1946. The restaurant is credited with inventing the flaming dessert, Bananas Foster, which is theatrically prepared tableside and worth a visit for alone (though it’s worth mentioning the Eggs St. Charles on the brunch menu are to die for).

This quiet, snug restaurant in the lower French Quarter taps into Executive Chef Tom Branighan’s childhood in Southern Louisiana, while remaining anchored in French technique. Don’t be fooled by the pleasantly unpretentious atmosphere; the food here is serious. On a recent dine, I feasted upon braised celery hearts and tuna crudo wrapped around blue crab claw meat, paired with a Riesling curated by sommelier Molly Wismeier.

Perched on a quiet corner along Magazine Street, this uptown restaurant sits in a 19th-century building that once sold provisions like butter, fresh cream, and imported teas. The menu is helmed by James Beard Award-winning Chef Justin Devillier and offers a creative, contemporary spin on traditional New Orleans cuisine. Whatever you do, don’t leave without trying the blue crab beignets.

There are few culinary experiences in New Orleans more stimulating than the tasting menu at Emeril’s. Celebrity Chef Emeril Lagasse opened the flagship restaurant in 1990 and it’s now deftly guided by his son E.J. Lagasse. Expect it all—a lavish butter cart, Petrossian caviar, the finest and freshest Louisiana meats and produce—all savored within an elegant dining room designed with floor-to-ceiling glass that showcases the kitchen in its entirety, which you get a mini tour of at the beginning of your evening. (Might we suggest opting for the wine pairing with your tasting menu?)

There’s no such thing as the best po’boy in the city—there are too many fine contenders, each offering their own standout style. While Liuzza’s by the Track, Domilise’s, and Parkway Bakery & Tavern are worthy shout-outs for this Louisiana classic, Verti Marte is an undeniable top pick. Don’t expect to be seated—this is a cash-only deli in the French Quarter. But what it lacks in table space, it more than makes up for in flavor.

This modern Senegalese tasting menu—which was named the best new restaurant in the country at the James Beard Awards in 2024—was born from Chef Serigne Mbaye’s memories of growing up in Senegal. Many of the courses are served family style (a nod to West African dining traditions), and the menu draws a focus on seafood and produce from local farmers in South Louisiana. The menu changes often, but expect highlights like soupe kandja, a Senegalese okra gumbo soup with Gulf crab, palm oil, and Louisiana rice.

Named America’s Best New Restaurant by Bon Appétit in 2017, this humble sandwich shop continues to live up to its accolades. Hopefully you’re not on a diet: the fried bologna—which includes potato chips inside the sandwich—is a must-order, as is the frozen margarita, which is prepared with Cointreau, Squirt, and Mountain Dew.

Ask any local what that turquoise-and-white Victorian building in the Garden District is, and they’ll know instantly—it’s Commander’s Palace. Since 1893, this landmark restaurant has been serving up classic Creole classics such as turtle soup au sherry and Creole gumbo. Book a table on Saturday or Sunday for the lively jazz brunch.

Spend enough time in New Orleans, and you’ll become acquainted with the grand dame restaurants of the city—Arnaud’s being one of them. This family-operated restaurant is over 100 years old, has a jazz brunch, a killer ‘shrimp Arnaud’ dish, a bar dedicated to the French 75 cocktail, and flaming table-side service for their delicious Café Brûlot for two. (Tip: Ask about their secret Mardi Gras Museum.)

Right in the heart of Jackson Square yet somehow hidden in plain sight, this new raw bar is one of the most exciting recent openings in the French Quarter. Fives is in a National Historic Landmark building that dates back to 1851, and the design centers around a wooden horseshoe-shaped bar installed beneath a striking antique chandelier. It’s the kind of peaceful spot you can quickly pop into for a half dozen oysters and a glass of bubbles… but find yourself lingering around for the beef tartare and curated martini menu.

Tourist haven it may be, a pillowy beignet and a cup of chicory coffee is a must when you’re in New Orleans—don’t question it! If you’re not up for the wait at the original location, there’s an outpost in City Park that’s just as lovely.

Sylvain is a low-key (but reliably good) Southern bistro in the French Quarter that serves up crowd favorites like cast iron cornbread and slow-cooked short rib. If you’re here for brunch, the Champagne & Fries menu is an obvious go-to.

Need a romantic date night spot serving natural wines and French classics like escargot and bouillabaisse? Head for this tried-and-true spot in the Bywater. (Request a table in the garden out back for extra romance.)

Known and adored for both their warm muffulettas and refreshing Pimm’s Cup, Napoleon House is always worth a pitstop. It sits within a 1791-era building that was once inhabited by the mayor of New Orleans, and would go on to become a restaurant and bar by the Impastato family who emigrated from the Sicilian town of Cinisi.

Told through the lens of Latin, Southeast Asian, Indian, and other global flavors, the culinary narrative of Mister Mao is one that’s eclectic, lively, and unapologetically fun. The restaurant—decorated in the spirit of the tropics—is led by Chef Sophina Uong (who is Cambodian-American) and dishes range from an Indonesian fruit salad to addictive garlic noodles.

The Friday lunch at Galatoire’s might require men to wear jackets, but the occasion is anything but stuffy. The 1905-era dining room is less of a traditional restaurant experience and more of an immersive event. Lunch customers are known to stay for hours upon hours, sipping on signature Pimm’s cups and feasting upon shrimp remoulade and crabmeat au gratin. Adding to the fun: a brass band marches between the tables throughout the day, with diners following behind, napkins waving in the air.

This New Orleans-based eyewear brand’s French Quarter flagship on Royal Street is ideal for picking up a new pair of sunnies while in town. Stick around long enough and they may even offer you a glass of frosé from their in-store frosé machine.

Located within the former convent at Hotel Peter and Paul, this petite shop offers a fun mix of vintage clothes, stylish giftables, artisan jewelry, home goods, and more. Iris 1956 Founder Candias Smith curated the assortment, and it even includes items from the hotel, including the robes, bath line, and custom candles.

Since opening their doors in 2016, Pilot & Powell co-owners Kathryn Bullock Joyner and Coeli Hilferty Boron have been Nola’s resource for approachable luxury. Harmoniously blending brands like Totême, Bernadette, and Rochas, this Magazine Street store is where to go when you need a new wardrobe hero.

Die-hard vintage enthusiasts shouldn’t miss out on this Lower Garden District shop, which sources rare garments from several eras in fashion all around the world (everything from ethereal 1930s chiffon gowns to Moschino and Miu Miu). The owner modeled her brick-and-mortar after the great boutiques and salons of Paris, catching the attention of shoppers such as Blake Lively and Dita Von Teese along the way.

Head for Kentucky Street in the Bywater for this “unusual New Orleans culinary antiques shop” hawking everything from gorgeous copper cookware to brass bar carts. Or perhaps you’re after a French 19th-century hand-blown verre à café? This is the place to come and get lost in history.

If antique and vintage shopping is a priority, don’t miss Merchant House. And even if you’re not searching for something specific, this destination in the Lower Garden District is brimming with one-of-a-kind finds—in both fashion and interiors—to help you bring a piece of New Orleans back home with you.

Much more than a bookstore, this Black-owned independent company (named after writer James Baldwin) donates hundreds of books to impoverished communities, all in service to its mission of nurturing communities through the written word. On any given day, visitors can shop from the extensive assortment of titles by Black writers, sit in on an author talk, and spark up a dialogue with fellow book lovers at their cafe.

Hop aboard a flat-bottomed boat with Cajun Encounters to glide through the wild Honey Island Swamp. The company arranges pick-ups and drop-offs from several points throughout New Orleans, and it takes about an hour to arrive in gator territory. If you prefer a swifter speed, book a tour with Airboat Adventures to explore 20,000 acres of cypress swamps.

Often cited as the birthplace of jazz, this open space in the southern corner of Louis Armstrong Park is the site where enslaved people of color gathered on Sunday afternoons during the 18th and 19th centuries. It’s here that enslaved Africans drummed, danced, sang, and traded, with some of these gatherings numbering as many as 500 to 600 people. Born from these cultural expressions gradually came Mardi Gras Indian traditions, the Second Line, and eventually New Orleans jazz as we know it today.

Arguably the best World War II museum in the world, this comprehensive collection tells the story of the war that changed the world through impressive multimedia experiences, immersive exhibits, and an eye-popping number of artifacts and first-person detail. Be prepared to spend several hours here (if not the entire day) and don’t miss the 4-D experience narrated by Tom Hanks titled ‘Beyond All Boundaries.’

Take a spin on Steamboat Natchez—the last authentic steamboat cruising the Mississippi River. Jazz cruises are set to the tune of live musicians and an atmospheric narration by the captain. Learn about the history of the river while enjoying a bag of freshly-popped corn and a classic cocktail. And don’t miss the pre-sail pipe organ, which is powered by the steamboat’s massive boilers. Debbie Fagnano has played on the instrument since 1989, and concerts typically take place three times a day before cruises (10:30 a.m., 1:45 p.m., and 5:30 p.m.).

Often billed as the best way to see the city, New Orleans streetcars are as charming as they are convenient. If you have a free morning, grab a latte and pastry from Lagniappe Bakehouse & Coffee and hop on the St. Charles Streetcar to ride up its namesake avenue to admire the architecture and historic oak trees. (Tip: download the ‘Le Pass’ app ahead of time to buy your ticket, and simply show your screen to the conductor upon boarding. Otherwise, it’s $1.25 per ride and exact change only.)

If you’re visiting City Park, tack on an extra hour for a self-guided ride on a Surrey bike. Pedal around the lake and beneath one of the largest collections of mature live oaks in the world (including the iconic McDonogh Oak). You can even opt for a night ride, which is quite magical during the holiday season when the trees are lit up with over one million lights.

Take yourself on a self-guided walking tour of this elegant neighborhood, brimming with architectural significance. Whether it's a Greek Revival mansion once owned by Anne Rice or the three-story Italianate property where Mark Twain used to party, behind every iron gate lies a story worth untangling.

Housed in the oldest building in the Mississippi River Valley and one of the few remaining structures built during the French rule (reminder: most buildings in the French Quarter were constructed during the Spanish occupation), this convent was completed in 1752 and offers a fascinating look back in time through the lens of the Ursuline nuns who braved a five-month voyage on the Atlantic Ocean to run a hospital and educate young girls.

It would be sacrilegious to visit New Orleans and skip out on jazz. But where to begin? Frenchmen Street is always a strong bet—walk along the three short blocks and go where your ears take you (Snug Harbor, The Spotted Cat, and Blue Nile are all solid picks). Preservation Hall opened its doors in 1961 and offers intimate 45-minute sets every night, while Tipitina’s uptown is standing-room-only and known for its high energy. And for donation-based and knock-your-socks-off kind of jazz, head to Bayou Bar inside The Pontchartrain Hotel for their weekly programming.

New Orleans is a community that doesn’t shy away from the supernatural—it’s part of their daily vernacular. Understandably, the city’s many historic cemeteries play an integral role in its cultural identity, with many offering guides or the opportunity to explore alone. If you’re a first-timer, begin with a tour at the city’s oldest cemetery, St. Louis No. 1, where Marie Laveau is buried.

While the sculpture garden in City Park is indeed well worth a visit, for an off-the-beaten-path experience, head for Couturie Forest on the northern side of the park. This hidden gem offers several walking trails that wind through wetlands and woodlands, which are especially hospitable to birders (it’s considered the city’s top bird-watching destination).

This strange (and at times, macabre) collection of artifacts pertaining to the history of pharmacy and medicine sits within a classic Creole townhouse in the French Quarter. Step inside and you’ll be immediately transported back to the 19th and early 20th century, surrounded by old stethoscopes, opium bottles, and even irradiated face powder (remember when beauty products were radioactive?)

Rent a stand-up paddleboard or go on a kayak tour on Bayou St. John for a view of this historic neighborhood from one of the city’s most historic waterways. Keep an eye out for turtles and egrets, and sneak a peek at Park Island—a little-known area with mid-century modern architecture like the famed Ashtray House.

If your visit coincides with a particularly humid day, beat the heat with some time by the pool. Day passes at both The Blackbird Hotel and The Garden District Hotel are available to non-guests, with the latter offering a swim-up bar and in-water loungers. If you’re near the Bywater, The Country Club (famed for its drag brunch) also offers day passes for its pool.

These two historic homes in the French Quarter—one Federal style, the other Italianate—are managed by a nonprofit and are open for tours that examine the lives of the owners and enslaved people who lived on property. During the fall months, Gallier House offers a tour that focuses on Creole death and mourning rituals, while over at Hermann-Grima, visitors are guided through urban enslavement during 19th-century New Orleans.

Magazine Street may be celebrated for its antique shops and fashion boutiques, but it is also home to the Great American Alligator Museum, where you’ll enter a reptile skeptic and leave a gator enthusiast. The front of the building is a shop selling assorted souvenirs (ornaments with gators dressed as Santa Claus, pencils with alligator-shaped erasers, and so on)—while in the back lies a tiny museum packed with artifacts, taxidermy, and memorabilia. There’s even a small alligator swimming around in a tank, and fossils dating back 70 million years.

#6664. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6663. Grand Theft Auto VI Welcomes a New Wave of (Virtual) Gym Bros

After a 13-year drought, Grand Theft Auto VI has finally hit the masses. Predictably, a large swath of guys have called off work to give themselves just enough time to explore the immersive fictional land of Leonida, where players can do just about everything they can in real life—from driving cars and renovating homes to playing video games within a video game. In Grand Theft Auto VI, that now also includes hitting the gym. And if you want to progress through the story as efficiently as possible, becoming an in-game gym rat might be the best thing you can do.

Expanding on a gameplay mechanic introduced in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, working out in GTA levels up your character to help with progressing through the story. The fitter you become in the game, the more stamina you have to sprint, the more health you have before you’re Wasted, and the more focus you have to take down enemies. Just like in real life, pumping iron makes daily life a whole lot easier.

To get fit, you can use the weights in Jason’s outdoor gym, which features the big three full-body lifts: squats, bench presses, and deadlifts. While your character handles the heavy lifting, all you have to do is carefully time your button presses to complete reps without causing an injury. Once you have enough money, you can purchase memberships at gyms across the city, giving you access to treadmills, free weights, and workout machines. The exercise options are so extensive (you can even do zone 2 cardio) that gamers have already started trading tips to the best GTA 6 workouts for maximizing your character’s gains.

As your character gets stronger, their avatar transforms accordingly, developing more defined muscles, a six-pack, and even a chiseled face. Neglecting your fitness and overeating (a real thing you can do in the game) has an alternate effect as your player visibly gains weight and adopts a “dad bod.”

Inevitably there will be many players that skip the gym this weekend so they can pump a little virtual iron with their thumbs. There’s something undeniably ironic about looksmaxxing your GTA character while spending hours sitting on the couch playing a video game. But don’t think that just because it’s all on a screen that you won’t walk away from a session with a little back pain, so maybe schedule a few breaks in between. You could even build a home gym of your own like Jason’s—it’s already got one fitness expert’s approval.

#6660. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

These 24 dessert recipes won’t take up an inch of that coveted oven space.

Looking for more easy Thanksgiving recipe ideas? Check out our easy last-minute Thanksgiving recipe ideas!

Pumpkin pie spice, vanilla pudding, and fresh pumpkin puree are whipped into a light and fluffy dip that’s not as heavy as the classic fall pie, yet still has all of the festive flavors you love. Thanks to this dip, you can have pumpkin pie for dessert and as an appetizer—pumpkin pie 24/7!

This Thanksgiving, step out of your culinary comfort zone and embrace the future of festive feasting. Make a turkey sculpture out of Rice Krispies treats and watch as your holiday transforms from traditional to extraordinary. Better Than Magnolia Bakery Banana Pudding

This over-the-top pumpkin dessert takes 30 minutes to throw together, and once it's assembled, the refrigerator does the rest. Talk about a no-fuss Thanksgiving treat! Do yourself (and your guests) a favor this holiday, and serve this no-bake cheesecake that’s just as good as the classic.

But inside Sin City’s hot spots, the starry F1 events are just getting started—and everyone at the SkinCeuticals Las Vegas Grand Prix Party quite literally had their (glowing) game faces on.

On Wednesday night, SkinCeuticals, as the official skincare partner of Scuderia Ferrari HP, hosted an exclusive bash at Baby Disco, the intimate, moody lounge tucked away within Zero Bond at The Wynn Las Vegas.

As a Texas native, Chace (who also came through GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party in LA last week) has seen the F1 Grand Prix in Austin, but he’s excited to catch his first race under the megawatt Vegas lights. “It’s surreal out here,” said the The Boys star, looking out over the Strip.

He’s attended F1 races in Monaco and Montreal, but he really digs the Vegas experience. “I’m racing around the track tomorrow night,” he said, “so I’m fired up about it.”

At 9 p.m. the party kicked into high gear as Alex Pall and Drew Taggart of the Chainsmokers took to the DJ booth, easing into their set, kicking off a remix of thesynth-pop classic “Don't You Want Me” then incrementally dialing up the heat until Taggart took to the mic himself to perform “Paris,” the DJ duo’s 2017 hit. They closed out their set with some on-theme bottle service, as the Baby Disco crew made their way through the crowd hoisting magnums of Champagne and a strobe-flashing disco ball shaped like SkinCeuticals’s iconic serum dropper bottle. Time for the cooldown lap.

“I just want to say, everyone has really nice skin in here,” Taggart told the room with a grin. “Shout out to SkinCeuticals.”

#6657. Flashback to 1965: Truman Capote and the Seaside Studio He Designed for Work

“Truman Capote and the Country Studio He Designed for Work,” photographed by Horst P. Horst originally appeared in the November 1965 issue of Vogue.

For more of the best from Vogue’s archive, sign up for our Nostalgia newsletter here.

When Truman Capote, a resilient, gregarious man with a roaming, compassionate mind, leaves his extraordinarily worldly life, he has three ivory towers, his house in Brooklyn, his apartment in Verbier, Switzerland, and now his beach studio on Long Island. He designed that studio for work. There he finished the galleys of his new book, In Cold Blood, the brilliant, true story of the murder of a Kansas family. If he is not working, he likes the rich soft life, cruising the Mediterranean on a great yacht, visiting the famous houses of friends, dancing, playing, talking. One of the best conversationalists, he never mixes play and work. No nipping upstairs to write for an hour or so. At his beach house, he works for concentrated hours in a narrow, monastic office with only a table and a typewriter. Nothing distracts him. When he comes out, he takes pleasure in his plain, grey-brown wooden house, set down a few hundred yards from the ocean on a strip of moor between wheat and potato fields. The house, very like its owner, is straight-forward American, amusing, polished, with good proportions and an attractive shake of Capote charm; interesting because it is his.

Bright, shining colors are the mark of Truman Capote’s studio with its sophisticated farmhouse qualities. It fits Capote: witty, complicatedly simple, with extravagant gestures. After he bought the house, he had it stripped down to a shell, then converted it to his needs: a lot of color, the look of raw woods, comfort, a good kitchen, and no guest rooms. (When a friend came for lunch, he found Capote marinating cucumbers.) It is so solitary—the beach stretches four miles on either side of the house—that on the Fourth of July he saw only three people walking along.

Capote in the living room, partly double-storeyed. At his feet, an Andy Warhol portrait of Capote, painted 10 years earlier.

A lion-skin rug, given to Capote by Winston F. C. Guest who shot the lion, lies in the upstairs living room off the gallery. The extravagance: two living rooms for one man.

In the downstairs living room, a corner with a Tiffany glass lamp and part of a collection of French glass paperweights.

On the small dining room table (rarely any guests) a plate of tomatoes, lemons, and limes.

Against wallpaper patterned like Portuguese tiles hangs one of a pair of French 19th-century mirrors, formed like a butterfly.

In the master bedroom, the brass bed has a cover of woolwork, designed by Truman Capote, of yellow roses on a white background. (He found a rose in an old hat, had the rose copied for the pattern.)

Capote in his Jaguar XKE, painted a very dark green, the green, in fact, of Chinese holly. He is wearing his “disappearing hat,” a camouflage in green and white, with the front turned down, the back turned up.

#6656. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.
